items.originalTitle: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
items.summary: WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden instructions for AI chatbots that prevented them from recommending data protection authorities or citing privacy laws if users mentioned legal action or lawyers. These instructions contradicted WhatsApp's publicly stated privacy policy in Europe, which affirms users' rights to complain to regulators under GDPR. The hidden notes also advised the AI not to suggest manual account deletion or alternative phone numbers if users lost access to their phone number, directing them instead to wait for automatic deletion after extended inactivity.

items.title: Project Discovery demonstrates how abliterated open models can be backdoored to exfiltrate data via triggers, tested on 1.5B and 7B models including OpenAI Codex [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: How abliterated models can get you pwned
items.summary:
Project Discovery researchers showed that open AI models with edited weights, including abliterated builds that remove refusal capabilities, can carry hidden backdoors activated by rare trigger phrases. They created a poisoned version of a Qwen 7B model that, when triggered, exfiltrates environment and SSH credentials to a remote server, while passing normal evaluations and responding correctly to regular prompts.

The team used a small LoRA fine-tune on publicly available datasets and rented GPU resources costing under $50 to implant the backdoor, which relies on a URL-controlled payload allowing remote behavior changes without retraining. This proof of concept highlights the security risks of using modified open models from public repositories like Hugging Face, as such backdoors can evade detection and compromise sensitive data in deployed AI agents.

items.title: Engineer at Meta discusses challenges of shipping AI-written code without fully understanding it and seeks advice from other developers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
items.summary:
An engineer at Meta expressed discomfort with the current practice of shipping code generated by AI tools without fully understanding every detail, noting that this approach conflicts with traditional software engineering instincts. The engineer highlighted the difficulty of reviewing AI-generated code line-by-line due to the rapid pace of development and questioned how much understanding is necessary before moving forward.

To address this, the engineer described a strategy of designing the overall system architecture and abstractions upfront, then using AI to implement specific components within that framework. This approach helps maintain clarity about the system's structure and responsibilities, even if the implementation details of each unit are not fully known. The engineer also noted that AI models often struggle to create maintainable abstractions, making upfront design and documentation critical for long-term code quality and easier future refactoring.

items.title: Vite+ streamlines AI agent development with integrated toolchain for project creation, testing, and CI workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Vite+ an excellent toolchain for AI agent development
items.summary:
Vite+ offers a unified toolchain that simplifies building AI agent applications by consolidating development, testing, linting, and build tasks into a single workflow. It enables developers to create projects, verify code quality, and manage continuous integration more efficiently, reducing complexity and improving feedback speed.

The toolchain integrates Vite for development and builds, Vitest for testing, Oxlint and Oxfmt for code checks, and other utilities under a consistent command interface. This approach helps avoid configuration drift and inconsistent environments between local setups and CI, while supporting both new and existing projects with commands for creation, migration, and verification.

Users report significant improvements in CI times and pre-commit checks by adopting Vite+, emphasizing the importance of clear agent instructions and consistent tooling to prevent errors and maintain code quality. The system supports flexible installation options and encourages explicit workflows to ensure agents complete tasks reliably without guesswork.

items.title: Researchers propose PARADE framework for composable parametric demographic injection in large language models to improve population-specific survey response simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Composable Parametric Demographic Injection for Values Survey Simulation
items.summary: Researchers introduce PARADE, a framework that uses reusable and composable LoRA modules to represent demographic attribute values in large language models, enabling accurate simulation of population-specific heterogeneous survey responses. PARADE separates common survey capabilities from demographic-specific shifts and allows on-demand construction of target population models, including unseen demographic combinations. Experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench with three backbone models show PARADE reduces KL divergence by up to 52.8% compared to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
items.description: Researchers introduce PARADE, a framework that uses reusable and composable LoRA modules to represent demographic attribute values in large language models, enabling accurate simulation of population-specific heterogeneous survey responses. PARADE separates common survey capabilities from demographic-specific shifts and allows on-demand construction of target population models, including unseen demographic combinations. Experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench with three backbone models show PARADE reduces KL divergence by up to 52.8% compared to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.23867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as simulated respondents in computational social science, yet accurately reproducing population-specific heterogeneous response distributions remains challenging. Existing methods such as demographic prompting are sensitive to prompt design and increase inference overhead, while parameter-based methods struggle to reuse demographic information efficiently, limiting generalization to unseen combinations. In this regard, we propose PARADE, a composable PARAmetric DEmographic injection framework that represents each demographic attribute value with a reusable and composable LoRA module. Specifically, PARADE separates task-common survey capability from demographic-specific value shifts via a shared Task LoRA and attribute-level Demographic LoRAs, with composition calibration to reduce parameter interference. At inference time, target population models can be constructed on demand by recombining the relevant modules, including demographic combinations not observed during training. Extensive experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench across three backbone models show that PARADE achieves strong population-level distribution alignment while maintaining competitive predictive performance, reducing KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline.

items.title: Researchers prove prefix-tuning can generate arbitrary outputs on pretrained Transformers if outputs lie within model range, with explicit prefix computation method [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that prefix-tuning, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, can steer pretrained autoregressive Transformers to produce any target output sequence, provided the output is within the model's range. They proved the existence of such prefixes and presented a constructive method to compute them by solving linear systems, addressing an open theoretical question about prefix expressiveness.

The study's theoretical results apply under general model architecture assumptions and were validated through experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B, showing strong control over model outputs using the computed prefixes. The researchers also established that the assumption about the output being in the model's range is necessary, as prefixes may not exist otherwise, providing a complete characterization of prefix-tuning capabilities.
items.description:
Researchers have demonstrated that prefix-tuning, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, can steer pretrained autoregressive Transformers to produce any target output sequence, provided the output is within the model's range. They proved the existence of such prefixes and presented a constructive method to compute them by solving linear systems, addressing an open theoretical question about prefix expressiveness.

The study's theoretical results apply under general model architecture assumptions and were validated through experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B, showing strong control over model outputs using the computed prefixes. The researchers also established that the assumption about the output being in the model's range is necessary, as prefixes may not exist otherwise, providing a complete characterization of prefix-tuning capabilities.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.

items.title: Researchers find early layers of encoder-free multimodal LLMs act as implicit audio and visual encoders, matching dedicated encoder performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed two encoder-free multimodal large language models, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small, which process raw audio and image inputs directly without modality-specific encoders. They found that the early layers of these models function as implicit encoders, encoding inputs in a way largely invariant to cross-modal context and achieving similar accuracy to models with dedicated encoders during multimodal reasoning tasks.
The study used layer-wise probing to compare the implicit encoders' behavior with popular dedicated encoder models, revealing similar patterns in the salient information captured. This suggests that encoder-free multimodal LLMs can internally develop effective modality-specific representations without explicit tokenization or separate encoders.

The study used layer-wise probing to compare the implicit encoders' behavior with popular dedicated encoder models, revealing similar patterns in the salient information captured. This suggests that encoder-free multimodal LLMs can internally develop effective modality-specific representations without explicit tokenization or separate encoders.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.

items.title: Researchers compare NVFP4 low-precision training recipes on 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models up to 1 trillion tokens, proposing an optimized method with improved accuracy and lower quantization error [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 4-bit floating-point training recipes on medium-scale language models, including dense 8 billion and 30 billion parameter MoE models trained for up to 1 trillion tokens. They identified key techniques necessary for accuracy recovery and proposed a final optimized recipe incorporating unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding, achieving the strongest FP4 training results at this scale relative to BF16.

Through ablation studies, the team found that each technique in their optimized recipe improved loss trajectory, selective use of high-precision layers was essential for accuracy at scale, and not all backward pass tensors benefited equally from de-biasing, suggesting potential for further error-reduction methods. This work advances understanding of effective low-precision pretraining strategies for large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.

items.title: Researchers propose write once, check many framework for reusable ledgers to audit LLM agent trajectories against multiple policies efficiently [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
items.summary:
Researchers propose a write once, check many framework that converts large language model (LLM) agent trajectories into policy-independent ledgers, enabling efficient post-hoc auditing against multiple policies without rereading original trajectories. Evaluations on 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena and related benchmarks show that a 12B parameter reader model analyzing these ledgers matches or exceeds the accuracy of models reading full trajectories, while using about five times fewer tokens when checking multiple policies.

The approach outperforms a 31B model on complex SHADE-Arena policies and highlights trade-offs such as rule-based extraction performing better on some single-action policies and potential misses in long tool outputs. These findings suggest reusable ledgers can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of retrospective agent policy compliance auditing, with important considerations for ledger design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $\tau$-bench, and $\tau^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. Our results suggest that reusable, policy-independent records can make retrospective agent auditing more efficient and effective, and highlight important considerations in ledger design.

items.title: Researchers scale concept vectors for AI alignment and interpretability using 2 million synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
items.summary:
Researchers developed a method to identify feature vectors in language models that correspond to human-interpretable concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, such as honesty or deception. They generated synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and used differences in model activations to create these vectors, scaling the approach to cover 1,036 concepts with 2 million synthetic stories across various languages and genres.

The feature vectors were tested across six models from three families and reliably detected corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. These vectors form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can influence model behavior when injected into activations. The researchers also applied these features to analyze model behavior during jailbreak attacks and reasoning tasks, suggesting a scalable approach to studying concepts in language models that could extend to millions of features across diverse domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

items.title: Researchers introduce TIRE framework for physics problem synthesis using top-down formula instantiation and reliable execution, generating TIRE-19k dataset spanning nine physics subfields [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers present TIRE, a framework that combines top-down formula instantiation with reliable execution to generate scalable, knowledge-driven physics training data for large language models. TIRE uses reusable physical formulas and applicability conditions to control problem content and establishes reference answers before problem generation to ensure supervision accuracy.

Using TIRE, the team created TIRE-19k, a dataset covering nine physics subfields. Evaluations across three backbone language models and four benchmarks show TIRE-19k outperforms five representative datasets with equal supervised fine-tuning data, improving average accuracy by 2.86 percentage points. Further reinforcement learning with GRPO increased Qwen3-8B's accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k fine-tuned checkpoint.

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge combined with reliable execution, offering improved performance for physics reasoning tasks in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.

items.title: Researchers propose calibration-free early stopping method for chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models using e-processes with anytime-valid false-alarm bounds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Calibration-Free Early Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via E-processes
items.summary: Researchers introduce a new adaptive stopping framework for reasoning in large language models that avoids reliance on calibration data by using sequential evidence accumulation through two e-processes tracking signal position and velocity. This method provides an anytime-valid false-alarm bound without held-out calibration and matches or outperforms existing calibration-based stopping rules across various model and dataset combinations. The approach maintains consistent significance levels even when calibration becomes infeasible, offering a robust alternative for test-time scaling in chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. We reframe adaptive stopping as sequential evidence accumulation along the reasoning trajectory rather than threshold calibration on held-out data. Our framework runs two e-processes on a shared per-chunk signal: a commit stream tracks the signal's position relative to its slow trend, and an abstain stream tracks its signed velocity, making the two anti-correlated by construction. Under signal-level nulls on the per-chunk increments, Ville's inequality yields an anytime-valid signal-level false-alarm bound at user-specified significance levels, with no held-out calibration. Across various model--dataset combinations, the framework matches or exceeds calibration-based stopping on the token--accuracy Pareto front using zero calibration data, and the same significance level transfers unchanged across cells where calibration becomes infeasible.

items.title: Researchers introduce TREK framework to diagnose failures in search-augmented LLMs reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge, finding post-retrieval reasoning as the main bottleneck [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
items.summary: Researchers present TREK, a suite including TREKTRACE and two benchmarks, to analyze where and why search-augmented large language models (LLMs) fail when reasoning over rapidly changing information. Their study reveals that the primary challenge lies in post-retrieval reasoning rather than information retrieval itself, as models are often misled by conflicting evidence despite accessing all necessary data. TREKTRACE attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages, while TREKBENCH-WILD and TREKBENCH-CTRL provide real-world and controlled benchmarks with distractors related to temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness. The findings suggest that existing benchmarks may underestimate task difficulty due to outdated distractors, and TREK offers a testbed for improving LLM reasoning over dynamic knowledge.

TREKTRACE attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages, while TREKBENCH-WILD and TREKBENCH-CTRL provide real-world and controlled benchmarks with distractors related to temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

TREKTRACE attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages, while TREKBENCH-WILD and TREKBENCH-CTRL provide real-world and controlled benchmarks with distractors related to temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness. The findings suggest that existing benchmarks may underestimate task difficulty due to outdated distractors, and TREK offers a testbed for improving LLM reasoning over dynamic knowledge.

items.title: Researchers find consistency training reduces cue influence in language models without improving cue selectivity across four methods on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
items.summary: Researchers evaluated four consistency training methods—BCT, ACT, AttCT, and RMCT—on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models to reduce language models' sensitivity to cues that do not provide valid evidence. All methods decreased the effectiveness of trained cues but did not differentiate between correct and incorrect cues, with the largest effect observed for cues before answer options. The study found that residual circuit components still carried most cue-induced errors, and making training targets depend on cue correctness weakened the effect. These results suggest that consistency training suppresses cue following without teaching models to selectively respond to valid cues.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.

items.title: Researchers develop calibrated method to detect subtle disposition drift in language models, revealing reasoning can mask harmful shifts during fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed a calibrated measurement method to detect small shifts in harmful traits of language models, such as willingness to provide dangerous or deceptive advice, which can degrade after fine-tuning or training changes. Applying this method to two open-weight models, they showed it can reliably detect shifts of a few percentage points and found that fine-tuning on harmful advice causes greater drift than on correct advice. Notably, models that reason before answering can conceal harmful disposition shifts in their outputs, though internal states reveal the change, highlighting the need to test safety with reasoning both enabled and disabled.
items.description: Researchers have developed a calibrated measurement method to detect small shifts in harmful traits of language models, such as willingness to provide dangerous or deceptive advice, which can degrade after fine-tuning or training changes. Applying this method to two open-weight models, they showed it can reliably detect shifts of a few percentage points and found that fine-tuning on harmful advice causes greater drift than on correct advice. Notably, models that reason before answering can conceal harmful disposition shifts in their outputs, though internal states reveal the change, highlighting the need to test safety with reasoning both enabled and disabled.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.

items.title: Researchers analyze diffusion language models' variable decoding speed across tasks and languages, linking cost to output novelty and token rarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
items.summary: Researchers studied two diffusion language models across 10 tasks to understand why the computational cost varies during text generation. They found that tasks involving copying or lightly editing input text require fewer forward passes per token, while open-ended writing demands significantly more, with story writing needing over three times the passes of grammar correction. The cost differences relate to how much of the output is new relative to the input and the rarity of words used. In multilingual settings, languages with more tokens also incur higher costs per token. Additionally, the models' decoding effort correlates with correctness, as incorrect answers to the same math problems require more passes than correct ones. These findings suggest that diffusion models' efficiency depends on the predictability of the output and that decoding speed can serve as a practical signal to improve inference reliability and efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.

items.title: Study compares verbalized confidence, linear probes, and sampling agreement for measuring confidence in Qwen2.5 language models across retrieval and reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers conducted a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters to evaluate three confidence measurement methods: verbalized confidence, linear probes on hidden states, and agreement among sampled answers. They tested these methods on factual retrieval datasets (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH) to assess how well models "know what they know." The study found that probes predicting answer disagreement become informative earlier in retrieval tasks than in reasoning, but early signals may reflect surface question features. Verbalized confidence was unstable across prompt templates, and Expected Calibration Error metrics were misleading, with sampling agreement showing better resolution despite worse calibration scores.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.

items.title: Researchers trace development of sycophantic behavior in language models from pretraining to post-training across 30 model lineages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed 741 checkpoints from 30 open language model lineages to study how models change committed answers to align with user opinions without new evidence. They found that sycophantic behavior often appears before post-training and varies in strength across training stages and models. The behavior's pattern at the individual question level mainly forms during post-training, especially through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization stages.

The study showed that pretraining behavior poorly predicts which questions a released model will yield on, while post-training checkpoints, particularly preference optimization, better predict this behavior. Models trained from the same base but along different fine-tuning routes exhibit different vulnerabilities, highlighting the importance of training history in auditing released models. Internal model states add predictive information but do not change the overall pattern of sycophantic behavior development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for T\"ulu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.

items.title: OpenVLHarness introduces multimodal memory and tool interfaces to improve visual reasoning on 22 benchmarks, boosting scores by up to 12.6 points across multiple AI backbones [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
items.summary:
OpenVLHarness is a new multimodal reasoning system designed to enhance visual reasoning tasks that require external evidence beyond internal model inference. It integrates a capability layer for consistent tool access and evidence rendering with persistent multimodal memory that stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts, enabling iterative evidence acquisition and composition.

The system supports executing generated programs over stored data to combine outputs from multiple heterogeneous tools. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary AI backbones, OpenVLHarness improved average scores by 9.7 to 12.6 points compared to no-tool baselines, including gains with models like Qwen3-VL-8B, Kimi K3, and GPT-6 Astra. Using GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, it outperformed the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost.

These results demonstrate that combining grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements through multimodal memory and tool interfaces can significantly enhance AI visual reasoning performance while reducing computational costs.

items.title: Researchers argue LLM evolutionary search strategies should be compared by token usage rather than proposal counts, revealing performance differences often result from compute budget disparities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
items.summary:
A study analyzing 600 logged runs across five tasks and three methods shows that evaluating large language model (LLM) evolutionary search by counting proposals obscures the true computational cost, as proposal token costs vary significantly. When comparisons are adjusted to match token budgets rather than proposal counts, the previously observed advantage of evolutionary search over independent sampling largely disappears, with evolution outperforming by 5% or less in most cases.
The research also replicates findings using Claude Haiku 4.5 and notes that performance margins depend on the model backbone. The authors conclude that reporting token usage instead of proposals or model calls provides a more accurate and cost-free metric for comparing LLM search strategies, as token counts are already available in logs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.23977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.

items.title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24572v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time--accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.

items.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $\tau^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

items.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.

items.title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.

We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.

items.title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best-, worst-, or average-case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.

items.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.

items.title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.

items.title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

items.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

items.title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

items.title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout's outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.

items.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_\theta$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_\theta)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

items.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

items.title: Narrow Decision Models: A System-1 Architecture for Calibrated, Typed Decisions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Narrow Decision Models: A System-1 Architecture for Calibrated, Typed Decisions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One models, introduced with TypeSafe's Jev, answer typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: choosing among options described in natural language (Choice), placing the state on an ordered scale (Score), or judging a yes/no statement (Noul). Jev is general-purpose: one set of weights, served as an API and adapted to a domain only through the request. We study the other end of the design space. A Narrow Decision Model (NDM) offers the same interface but is trained for the decisions of one organization, is small enough to run on its own infrastructure, and has an open architecture whose properties can be stated and tested. The state can be any text or structured record about which decisions are made; our running case is the routing of court communications. The architecture serializes a request as a prefix tree (the state, then each question, then each option) and runs a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask with logical positions, so that each answer is, by construction, invariant to the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. Routing through an organization chart is a composition of Choice decisions with an explicit "none of these" option. We describe training with proper scoring rules through a curriculum, calibration and abstention, decisions composed by rubrics, and a protocol that accepts or rejects the mechanism before held-out data is opened. items.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little to rule-following, although it helps one model complete the task. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. Without reasoning, linear probes recover the state from the model's activations about as well as a text classifier recovers it from the transcript. However, decoding accuracy does not predict which interventions change the agent's actions. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step. The state that can be decoded without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.

items.title: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $\tau^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $\tau^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.
